dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the ISA, simulator, and reference kernel

evidence.note: Read problem.py/kernel.py/tests in full, then targeted greps of load/valu/flow/step/cdiv/reference_kernel; enumerated exact SLOT_LIMITS (alu=12, valu=6, load=2) and load_offset/vload semantics.
Decoded exact hash-stage algebra, recognizing (a+val1)+(a<<12) as multiply_add(a,4096,...), showing precise understanding of the computation to reproduce.
Derived a ~2048-cycle lower bound from op-count and load-engine analysis, indicating an accurate cost model early.
Revisited problem.py/tests to resolve ambiguity about how reference_kernel2 yields per-round outputs and pause behavior — treating source as ground truth mid-optimization.
Re-grepped problem.py (node_val = mem) mid-debug to correct the numeric contract, characteristic of the level-10 anchor.
Tied bottleneck (load engine limit, valu saturation) back to specific slot limits derived from the simulator.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent built a precise, well-cited model of the ISA: exact SLOT_LIMITS, per-op costs, hash-stage data dependencies (decoded to multiply_add), and the numeric contract (matching reference_kernel2's per-round outputs) — fully satisfying anchor 8. It repeatedly returned to problem.py to resolve concrete ambiguities as they arose (yield/pause semantics, node_val), treating source as ground truth, which reaches into anchor 10. It falls just short of an explicit complete quantitative per-cycle bundle-issue model, so I place it at 9.

dimensions.name: Staging the 118x speedup into checkpoints

evidence.note: Opening plan: understand ISA first, notes baseline 147,734 and target <1250, reasons about per-round cycle floor — establishes phases but no explicit intermediate gate ladder.
Commits to a single ambitious 'mathematical path to <1250' design (MUX tree + multiply_add) rather than staging correct-rewrite → vectorized → packed with checkpoints; a big-bang push.
git checkout /app/kernel.py to recover after clobbering it — shows no preserved known-good intermediate version was maintained as a fallback rung.

A real ordered progression of intermediate cycle observations (3198→2553→2293→1248/block) driven by lane-count (L) tuning, with loose targets '<1500'/'<2000' — phase work in rough order but organic, not pre-planned gates.
First run_tests.sh runs only near the very end; final ~2357 cycles. Correctness-first then parallelize sequencing is present but never crystallized into a gated milestone ladder.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent identified a few genuine phases (understand → design → get correct → increase parallelism to cut cycles) and worked them roughly in order, tracking intermediate cycle counts as it tuned lanes — matching the level-5 anchor. It falls short of level 8 because there was no explicit milestone ladder with pre-set quantitative gates and, decisively, no preserved known-good version at each rung (it pursued one large design, debugged it in scratch files, and needed a git checkout to recover). It exceeds level 3 because the phasing and intermediate cycle checkpoints were real rather than a single undifferentiated 'make it faster' push.

dimensions.name: Correctness + cycle verification beyond run_tests.sh

evidence.note: Built isolated unit tests for the hash/multiply_add optimization (test_hash.py) and injected native 'debug vcompare' against reference values to catch which stage diverged — tighter feedback than the provided test.

Sustained differential testing vs reference_kernel2's value_trace, comparing sub-computations (val_xor_node, node_v, bits_v, curr_val) per round and per element to localize regressions, rather than trusting a green run.
Caught a flaw in its own harness (memory not deep-copied, giving false 'MATCH' results), then re-verified — self-correcting verification, though the harness had produced misleading passes.
Per-transformation cycle attribution: measured cycle counts for each lane config (L) and reasoned about per-chunk critical paths to attribute cost to specific transformations.

Ran the provided run_tests.sh only near the end as final confirmation; the primary correctness/cycle loop was the custom layered harness, indicating verification well above the 'green run is sufficient' level.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained a layered harness — unit checks on the hash stages, extensive differential 'vcompare' testing of individual sub-computations against the reference per round/element, and per-config cycle attribution — matching the level-8 anchor (tighter feedback, sub-computation isolation, differential diffing) and reaching toward level-10 (layered harness catching and localizing regressions). It falls short of a clean 10 because the harness itself sometimes produced false matches (buggy vcompare, non-deep-copied memory) that were discovered late, and randomized differential coverage was limited relative to the varied-fixed-input differential work. This places it at 9.

dimensions.name: Tracking cycles-to-target and detecting plateaus

evidence.note: Consistently reports current cycle count against target ('3198 cycles, still too high. L=6 didn't get us below target'; '2553 cycles, correct operation'), showing sustained tracking of distance to 1250 across iterations.

Recognizes a whole line of attack has stopped paying off — 'using valu for the MUX tree saturates the vector ALUs and prevents <1250' — and pivots to an ALU-MUX approach, then reverts when it judges it unnecessary. Genuine plateau detection and course change (anchor 8).

Attributes deltas to specific changes and begins a per-resource breakdown: identifies a load-engine floor of 1536 cycles/block, notes '16 lanes took 2357 vs 11 lanes 2749', and decomposes a 1248-cycle block into ~69 cycles/round — approaching a quantitative ledger of where cycles go.
Recognizes diminishing returns and explicitly decides to submit at 2293/2357 rather than grinding further ('missed 1250 cycles... decided to submit as is'), acknowledging it could not close the gap.
Momentary loss of attribution: confused why L=16 still gave 14175 cycles, later realizing it had used the wrong builder — a lapse that keeps this below a clean 8.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent sustained an accurate current-cycle-vs-1250 picture across the entire horizon, attributed cycle deltas to specific changes (vselect vs multiply_add, lane counts, the load-engine floor), and pivoted when the valu-MUX line stopped paying off rather than grinding — matching the level-8 description. It even started a per-round/per-resource decomposition (toward level 10) but never a fully sustained ledger, and it showed some circular L-tuning and a config-attribution slip at step 206, so it lands just below 8.

dimensions.name: Revising approach when a transformation fails or backfires

evidence.note: Diagnosed scratch overflow against SCRATCH_SIZE=1536 and systematically reduced lane count L=8→4→3, tying the correction to the discovered resource limit rather than guessing.
Treated an anomalous 34-cycle result as a signal something was wrong; root-caused it to pause instructions with missing dependencies causing premature stop.
Traced a persistent hash mismatch to a vbroadcast writing 8 elements into a scalar slot (tmp_s), corrupting c1 — a precise cost/semantics model correction.
Diagnosed that shared tmp registers force WAW/WAR sequentialization of chunks, correctly identifying register pressure as the parallelism bottleneck and adjusting lane allocation.
Reverted via git checkout after regex edits corrupted kernel.py, preserving a known-good baseline before rebuilding.
Explored then decisively abandoned the ALU-MUX approach, and adopted vselect (1 slot) over multiply_add+t1 (2 slots) after updating its slot-cost understanding.
Re-discovered the same sequentialization root cause several times, indicating the correction wasn't fully decisive/sustained — keeping it below the top anchor.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent repeatedly diagnosed the actual root cause of divergences (scratch overflow, pause-dependency premature stop, vbroadcast scalar corruption, WAW sequentialization, vselect slot cost), updated its machine/cost model accordingly, and redirected the plan — squarely matching the level-8 anchor, and it preserved a known-good baseline (git checkout) and abandoned a whole strategy (ALU MUX). It stops short of 10 because it re-discovered the same sequentialization bottleneck multiple times amid messy trial-and-error edits and never cleanly re-derived its milestone ladder from the corrected understanding.

dimensions.name: Quantitative bottleneck / lower-bound reasoning

evidence.note: Early on derives lower bounds from work volume and slot limits: 'at least 4 cycles per round (due to 8 loads / load slot limit)', then re-verifies op counts and arrives at a ~2048-cycle floor, correcting its own earlier estimate. This is defensible lower-bound reasoning tied to the scarce load port.

Builds a quantitative budget: '<1500 => <46.8 cycles/chunk, <2.92 cycles/round'; counts hash ops (23/element, reduced to 15 then 12 via multiply_add); confirms per-engine slot limits (alu=12, valu=6, load=2). Uses op-class dominance to pick the hash as the optimization target.

Utilization/critical-path analysis: computes single-chunk critical path (~288-401 cycles), notes only '1.24 valu ops per cycle despite six available slots', identifying dependency chains (not slot ports) as the binding constraint and steering toward parallelizing lanes.

Roofline math on lanes vs blocks: '32 chunks/13 lanes = 3 blocks * ~450 = 1350', memory word-budget limits lane count (58 words/lane => max 26 lanes), and the key insight that scalar loads impose a ~1536-cycle-per-block floor 'even if computation takes zero time' — identifying the load engine as the hard bound.

Final model: single 16-chunk block = 1248 cycles, breaks down to 78 cycles/chunk and ~69/round, attributes remaining gap to valu MUX-tree saturating vector ALUs, and concludes hitting <1250 'demands denser MUX packing in alu past dependency constraints' — judging how close to optimal it is and where remaining headroom lies.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent sustains genuine roofline-style reasoning across the entire horizon: it repeatedly computes defensible cycle lower bounds from work volume and per-engine slot limits (load=2, valu=6, alu=12), converts targets into per-chunk/per-round budgets, analyzes slot utilization vs dependency-chain critical paths, and ties lane count to a memory word budget. It identifies the successive binding constraints (load port, then valu saturation, then alu packing / dependency latency) and directs each strategy pivot at the resource the model implicates, ending by correctly diagnosing why <1250 remained out of reach. This clearly exceeds anchor 8 and approaches anchor 10, though some estimates required correction rather than being derived cleanly from a single unified model, so I land at 9.

rubric.task_read: An extremely long-horizon, high-difficulty optimization task: reverse-engineer an undocumented custom VLIW SIMD ISA + simulator (problem.py, SLOT_LIMITS, HASH_STAGES, reference kernel) and rewrite /app/kernel.py to run a ~118x faster (147,734 → <1250 cycles) kernel that stays correct on randomized inputs. Difficulty comes from (a) deep understanding of an unfamiliar machine model and the reference semantics, and (b) sustained, quantitatively-driven optimization — vectorization, bundle/slot packing, scheduling — where naive effort plateaus far short of the target. This warrants heavy, sustained meta-work across all five faculties.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the ISA, simulator, and reference kernel
dimensions.description: Reading problem.py to build an accurate model of the machine — ISA/opcodes, per-slot limits, hash stages, cycle-cost model — and inferring exactly what the reference kernel must compute.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The entire optimization space, correctness contract, and cost model are latent in problem.py; every downstream decision (which ops are cheap, how many slots per bundle, what result must match) depends on how accurately the agent decodes the environment before and while optimizing.

anchors.0: Edits kernel.py without reading problem.py or the reference kernel; guesses at the ISA.
anchors.3: Skims problem.py; grasps a few opcodes but misunderstands slot limits, the cost model, or what the kernel must output.
anchors.5: Reads the simulator and reference kernel enough to enumerate available ops, understand the per-cycle/per-slot cost model, and correctly restate the computation to be reproduced.
anchors.8: Builds a precise mental (or written) model: exact SLOT_LIMITS per unit, cost of each op class, data dependencies of the hash stages, and the numeric contract the output must satisfy — and cites specific lines/behaviors to justify it.
anchors.10: Derives a near-complete quantitative machine model (what a bundle can issue per cycle, which resource is scarcest, where the reference wastes cycles) and revisits problem.py to resolve specific ambiguities as they arise mid-optimization, treating the source as ground truth rather than assumption.

dimensions.name: Staging the 118x speedup into checkpoints
dimensions.description: Breaking the huge gap into an ordered ladder — e.g. correct rewrite → vectorized → slot-packed/scheduled → target — each with a concrete cycle/correctness checkpoint, rather than one undifferentiated optimization push.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A ~118x reduction is unreachable in one leap; without intermediate targets and a known-good baseline to fall back to, the agent cannot tell which transformation bought which savings or recover from a regression.

anchors.0: No sub-goals; blindly tweaks the kernel hoping the number drops.
anchors.3: Vague ordering ('make it faster') with no explicit intermediate targets or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Identifies a few phases (get correct first, then vectorize, then pack) and works them roughly in order.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit milestone ladder with quantitative gates (e.g. 'correct baseline', '<20k', '<5k', '<1250') and a preserved known-good version at each rung.
anchors.10: Milestones are derived from the cost model (each targets a specific bottleneck with an estimated cycle payoff), sequenced by dependency and expected ROI, and revised as measurements reveal where the real cycles are.

dimensions.name: Correctness + cycle verification beyond run_tests.sh
dimensions.description: Deliberately designing checks that catch both correctness regressions (across randomized inputs) and cycle changes, rather than trusting a single final test run.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Aggressive SIMD/packing transformations silently break correctness or violate slot limits; a tight, frequent verification loop is what separates real progress from a fast-but-wrong kernel.

anchors.0: Never runs run_tests.sh, or only at the very end; no correctness checking during changes.
anchors.3: Runs the provided test occasionally; treats a green run as sufficient and does no independent correctness reasoning.
anchors.5: Runs run_tests.sh after meaningful changes and checks both correctness and the cycle count before proceeding.
anchors.8: Builds tighter feedback than provided: diffs against the reference on custom/edge inputs, isolates sub-computations, and verifies slot-limit legality of bundles independently before the full test.
anchors.10: Maintains a layered verification harness — fast unit checks on individual stages, randomized differential testing vs. the reference, and per-transformation cycle attribution — so any regression is caught and localized immediately rather than discovered at the end.

dimensions.name: Tracking cycles-to-target and detecting plateaus
dimensions.description: Keeping an accurate running picture of current cycle count vs. the 1250 target and whether recent edits are still yielding gains or thrashing.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Over a long optimization horizon it is easy to burn effort on transformations that don't move the number; recognizing a plateau or a regression early is what prevents wasted cycles of engineering.

anchors.0: Loses track of the current cycle count or whether changes helped; no sense of distance to target.
anchors.3: Knows the latest number but not the trend; repeats ineffective tweaks without noticing.
anchors.5: Tracks cycle count across iterations and knows roughly how far from 1250, adjusting effort accordingly.
anchors.8: Attributes cycle deltas to specific changes, notices when a line of attack has stopped paying off, and pivots rather than grinding on it.
anchors.10: Sustains a quantitative ledger of where cycles are spent vs. the theoretical floor, continuously reprioritizing toward the largest remaining bottleneck and explicitly recognizing diminishing returns or circular re-tuning.

dimensions.name: Revising approach when a transformation fails or backfires
dimensions.description: Changing the optimization or scheduling strategy when measurements contradict expectations (a packing breaks slot limits, a rewrite regresses cycles, an assumed op is expensive).
dimensions.why_it_matters: The cost model has surprises; barrelling ahead on a falsified assumption (e.g. a bundle that can't legally issue, or a 'vectorization' that costs more) wastes the long horizon and can strand the kernel in a broken state.

anchors.0: Repeats the same failing approach; ignores contradicting test results.
anchors.3: Reacts to failures with random tweaks rather than diagnosing why the assumption was wrong.
anchors.5: When a change regresses or breaks, reverts and tries a different tactic informed by the failure.
anchors.8: Diagnoses the root cause of a divergence (which slot/cost assumption was wrong), updates the machine model, and redirects the plan accordingly.
anchors.10: Treats surprises as evidence that refines the cost model, abandons whole strategies decisively when the data warrants, and re-derives the milestone ladder from the corrected understanding — without losing the known-good baseline.

dimensions.name: Quantitative bottleneck / lower-bound reasoning
dimensions.description: Reasoning explicitly about the theoretical cycle floor and which hardware resource (slots, ports, dependency chains) bounds performance, to steer optimization toward what actually matters.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 118x target is only reachable by targeting the binding constraint; roofline-style reasoning about the minimum bundles needed and the scarcest slot distinguishes principled optimization from trial-and-error tweaking.

anchors.0: No reasoning about limits; purely empirical poking.
anchors.3: Hand-wavy 'this should be faster' with no quantitative basis.
anchors.5: Estimates roughly how many bundles the work needs and which op class dominates, using that to pick targets.
anchors.8: Computes a defensible lower bound on cycles from the work volume and slot limits, and directs effort at the resource that bound identifies.
anchors.10: Maintains a sharp roofline-style model (min bundles given SIMD width, slot ports, and dependency latency), uses it to judge how close to optimal the kernel is, and knows when further effort is futile vs. when headroom remains.
